iterations.theme: Modern dating and approaching: who approaches first, signs of interest, brakes and the first date

sections.subtitle: A topic the editorial team did not plan: modern dating and who approaches first
sections.screenshot_description: Host in the studio at the start of the Generacija plus show, in frame with the LaudatoTV logo
sections.content:
The show **Generacija plus** on **LaudatoTV** opens with the host's greeting, in which he announces a new topic to viewers. The host points out that the editorial team never planned to deal with this topic, but that it is, in his words, necessary because of social circumstances and because of what everyone is surrounded by. The subject is **modern dating** and the question of how guys approach girls.

The host admits he has no extensive introduction prepared because the participants themselves do not know in advance where the conversation will go. He does, however, name the main questions: who should approach first, how to recognize whether a contact is heading in a good direction, and whether one should “push” things by force. He emphasizes that this is enough for a start and that the conversation will develop throughout the show.

The host then announces the structure of the conversation in several phases: signs of interest, the process of approaching itself, so-called **red flags**, unrealistic expectations, and what the first meeting should be. This sets the framework for the whole episode.

sections.subtitle: Does a girl give a sign, and should a guy approach first?
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 1 speaks at the table while the host holds notes; the frame shows the title of the segment on signs of interest
sections.content:
The host opens the question of signs of interest: how a guy can know that a girl likes him, or how to recognize that it is necessary to take the first step. **Female Guest 1** (Guest 1) then offers an observation from conversations with her friends. According to her, many young men say they will not approach a girl until they notice that she is sending them some sign.

The female guest considers such an attitude sad. She says she could not sleep peacefully herself if she had not tried something, even when the girl did not give a clear sign. She points out that it is easy for her to say this precisely because she speaks from a female perspective, and she asks whether men can really remain passive if they have received no signal at all.

**Guest 2** replies that it is more natural and easier for interest to develop in some kind of social gathering or through occasional meetings, when there is contact and at least basic getting to know each other. Even a look can be a beginning. However, he emphasizes that if he liked a girl, it would be good to approach her regardless of whether there were earlier return signals.

**Guest 3** adds that clear, visible openness is important. He describes a situation in which a girl avoids eye contact or quickly looks away, which can be a clear indication of disinterest. He emphasizes that he personally would not approach a girl based only on attraction, but would first want to get to know her character, and only then, once that has happened, think about the first step.

sections.subtitle: Gaze, words and body: how to read signals in a conversation
sections.screenshot_description: Close-up of the female guest explaining, with a shot of two young people talking in a café as an illustration
sections.content:
The host asks what the real signs of interest are, because in men's circles one often hears that a girl looked at a guy the whole evening or that “she surely likes him,” and yet nothing comes of it. The host names two situations: first, one in which two people meet and immediately feel attraction, and second, one in which they get to know each other through prayer communities, mutual friends and social gatherings.

**Female Guest 1** considers a look an important sign, but says it should not be overestimated. If two people look at each other the whole evening, that is not something to dismiss, but the problem is that often nobody takes the next step. According to her, the situation is at its worst when both sides are waiting for the other to begin.

The female guest goes on to explain that real signals show only in conversation. It does not have to be anything spectacular, but ordinary, casual communication. What is key is to notice how the other person reacts: whether they answer with just one word or continue the conversation, whether they smile, whether they ask questions. It is precisely these **verbal and nonverbal signs** that reveal real interest.

The host then refers to the biblical principle that a sign should not be given in any way other than what the person themselves shows, thereby warning about caution in interpreting other people's messages.
keywords: context of getting to know each other

sections.subtitle: When politeness deceives: loss of signals and awkward moments
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 2 and Female Guest 1 in conversation, with emphasis on gestures and posture
sections.content:
**Guest 2** warns that in practice girls differ. Some tend to accommodate others, so they may prolong a conversation out of politeness, even when the person is not attractive to them. Others will clearly show disinterest. That is why reading signals is not always simple.

**Female Guest 1** adds that it is important for guys to be aware of body language, and for girls to be aware of their own behavior. Many men, she says, pester girls and do not understand that their interest is not reciprocated. Girls often will not confront them directly, but will be polite while giving short answers.

As concrete indicators, the female guest mentions a situation in which a girl turns away from the person she is talking to, constantly looks somewhere else, answers only with “yes” or “no,” and asks no follow-up questions. Such behavior, in her view, can be a clear sign that interest is not high and that it is time to withdraw.

sections.subtitle: Physical attraction as a foundation or superficiality?
sections.screenshot_description: Host speaks in front of the camera; on screen the caption “Physical attraction”
sections.content:
The host introduces the topic of physical attraction and presents the view that it is the foundation of every approach to a girl. He admits that he cannot fall in love with a person who is not physically attractive to him, although he notes that the soul and inner qualities are also valued. He states that, in his opinion, there is no point in starting contact with someone who does not attract him physically.

He adds that people who are not attractive to him, even with a good character, are among the reasons he gives up on contact. As an example, he mentions a situation in which he would argue with someone who is not physically attractive to him, which, in his words, would further reduce his interest.

The host also announces that questions of ugliness and aesthetics will be addressed in another show, which emphasizes that this is an introduction to the topic of attraction and not its complete analysis.

sections.subtitle: Fear of rejection: is it the worst thing in the world?
sections.screenshot_description: Female Guest 1 explains her attitude toward rejection, with a shot from the studio
sections.content:
The host asks whether girls are to blame if guys do not approach them, and whether the reason lies in their behavior or in the fact that the guys simply failed. **Female Guest 1** does not think that only the girls are to blame. She points out that it is wrong to mock rejection and to spread stories about it, because this unnecessarily humiliates the person who tried.

In this regard the female guest shares a personal experience, stressing that rejection was not the worst thing that ever happened to her. She believes that fear of rejection is stronger among young men than among young women, and that this is precisely why many give up before they even try.

She adds that it matters how rejection is expressed. If a girl is normal and polite, she should not laugh at someone who approached her. If, on the other hand, she is rude, it is better that such a person not be a partner. The female guest stresses that she personally holds great respect for anyone who bravely shows interest, even if they receive the answer “no,” whereas someone who told her they liked her but never did anything about it would seem to her like a coward.

sections.subtitle: A male or female job: who approaches first today?
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 3 and Female Guest 1 in a debate on the roles of the sexes in getting to know each other
sections.content:
The host asks who approaches first today, girls approaching boys or the reverse, and whether the first contact is a male task or whether women can also initiate it. The answers are varied.

**Guest 3** considers initiative to be a male task. He shares a personal experience in which a girl approached him herself, which was not pleasant for him and did not match his character. In his opinion, the more concrete step, such as inviting someone on a date, should be taken by the man. Still, he agrees that a woman can, in a subtle way, create a situation in which the man will approach.

Female Guest 1 sees things differently. She would not initiate a relationship herself, because she would then feel that she was responsible for its beginning and that it would follow her. According to her, some of her friends think it would be easier if a girl approached them, while others would find that unusual.

The host expresses strong opposition to female initiative, stating that he sees such a move as an expression of desperation, although he notes that he is speaking personally and does not want to belittle anyone. He adds that in that case he would have to take on the role of the man in the relationship, which would not be acceptable to him.

sections.subtitle: Summer camps and prayer communities as an opportunity to get to know people
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 3 speaks about shared gatherings; on screen the caption “Camps and communities”
sections.content:
Guest 3 points out that people in communities are often closed off, although the best opportunities to get to know people with similar beliefs arise at camps and gatherings. He calls for openness and for awareness that getting to know someone can happen even when that is not the primary goal.

As an example, he mentions a friend who waited at a wedding for someone to invite him to dance, while two women simply got up on their own and started dancing. According to him, such situations show that waiting can be a clear message of passivity.

The host then proposes, quite sharply, that summer camps be closed to people who are in a relationship, with the view that someone who is in a relationship should not look for new friends at such events, but should devote themselves to prayer and to preparation for marriage. He presents this claim as his personal opinion and admits that some situations in which people look for partners in a church setting do not appeal to him.

sections.subtitle: Brakes on approaching: the internet, anonymity and pornography
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 4 speaks in front of the camera; on screen the caption “What holds back approaching?”
sections.content:
The host introduces the topic of brakes on approaching, especially among men. He asks why it is much easier to send a message on Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat or Facebook than to approach a person in person. He adds that the online world offers an abundance of options, which often leads to superficiality.

**Guest 4** points out that courage shown on the internet is false. Anonymity makes it possible to carefully compose a message and send it without really facing a reaction. According to him, young people are reluctant to expose themselves to awkwardness, so they choose the easier path.

For comparison, he notes that in the past the first contact required a letter, which meant waiting a long time and thinking things over many times. Today everything is instant. Guest 4 believes that pornography further affects the way men look at women, because it creates unrealistic expectations and reduces the willingness to establish real contact. He calls this a major problem for young people.

**Guest 3** adds that the digital age makes people less practiced in practical communication. People, he says, increasingly experience social situations as a project that must be planned in advance, which diminishes naturalness and ease.

sections.subtitle: Reaching out on social networks and creating circumstances
sections.screenshot_description: Female Guest 1 and Host in conversation about reaching out online; social media icons on screen
sections.content:
Female Guest 1 holds the view that social networks are not necessarily bad and that many couples formed exactly that way: someone reached out online and a relationship developed. She herself has nothing against someone reaching out to her via the internet.

The host asks whether it is good to reach out to an unknown person on a social network. Female Guest 1 replies that this is a different matter, while the greater sense lies in reaching out to a person whom someone already knows but did not have the courage to approach in person. It is precisely here that the host sees the main problem: lack of initiative.

The host emphasizes that if he liked a girl, he would create the circumstances for a meeting himself. According to him, some will do this, and some will always find an excuse. Female Guest 1 agrees that the answer depends most on how much and how a person really appeals to the other, and that fear is often the main obstacle.

The host concludes that he cannot imagine someone approaching a random person on a social network just on the basis of a profile, which, in his opinion, is not normal.

sections.subtitle: Lack of social skills: men who struggle to connect
sections.screenshot_description: Host speaks about football training; on screen the caption “Social skills”
sections.content:
The host states that one psychologist pointed out that men today develop social skills poorly, and not only in contact with women but also among themselves. As an example, he describes football sessions where players barely greet each other, arrive, play and leave, with no real connection.

In his words, men are weakly connected to other men in terms of life, which is why it is also hard for them to approach women. This lack of friendly connection, he believes, contributes to fear and insecurity in situations of getting to know someone.

The host concludes this point by announcing that he will go on to list several more brakes that he noted during the conversation.

sections.subtitle: Shame, sacrifice and exclusivity: three of the hardest brakes
sections.screenshot_description: Host lists the brakes on paper or on screen; the caption “Shame – sacrifice – exclusivity” is shown
sections.content:
The host names three additional brakes that he considers especially important. The first is **shame**. Many young men, he says, feel shame and fail to overcome it, so they do not approach girls, even when they have the chance. Shame is intensified by fear of failure or of a situation in which things turn out not to be as they hoped.

The second brake, which the host considers even more pronounced, is the awareness that a relationship requires **readiness for change and for sacrifice**. In his opinion, many men today are not prepared to give up their own habits and adapt to another person, so they do not enter into a relationship.

The third brake is the absence of **exclusivity**. The host believes that today's male gaze is often unfaithful, due to the influence of pornography and social networks, where a woman can be compared with countless others. As a solution he proposes that the first and basic rule in a relationship be based on exclusivity, that is, on the decision to choose one person and remain faithful to them, regardless of whether there are others who might perhaps be more beautiful, more intelligent or more pious.

The host concludes that such determination and devotion, in his conviction, can be blessed.

sections.subtitle: Red flags: what the guests consider problematic in a guy
sections.screenshot_description: Female Guest 1 speaks about indicators of a problematic partner; on screen the caption “Red flag”
sections.content:
The host introduces the popular term **red flag** and asks the female guests and guests what they consider problematic in a guy today.

**Female Guest 1** names a lack of initiative as a major minus. As an example, she describes a situation in which a guy invites someone on a date but does not know where they will go or has planned nothing. She stresses that the girl should also take part, but that the man should show initiative. She extends this thought to passivity and lack of ambition: a man should have a desire for work and earnings and be capable of supporting a family. If he does nothing and lives at someone else's expense, such passivity is off-putting to her.

**Guest 4** and other participants add that it is important how a guy behaves toward others. According to him, kindness toward waiters, delivery people and salespeople says more about character than behavior toward people from whom one is gaining something. Caring for oneself is also important: excessive focus on one's own appearance can be off-putting, as can complete neglect of oneself, which may indicate a future inability to care for others.

The host concludes this part by saying that the proposals are clear, but still need to be developed more concretely.

sections.subtitle: Family as a mirror of character
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 4 explains the importance of family relationships; family role names are shown in the frame
sections.content:
The host asks what the guests consider problematic, and what they look for in girls and in relationships. **Guest 4** replies that a good relationship with family is very important, primarily with parents, but also with other family members and with people in general. In his opinion, this says something about a person's spiritual background and maturity.

Guest 4 explains that a healthy family usually produces healthy people, and that people are often a picture of their parents and of the way they were raised. Of course, he adds, Jesus can change lives, but upbringing remains a strong foundation. That is why it is important to him to see how a girl grew up and what she went through in her family. If he notices something suspicious, that is a sign for him to be cautious.

**Guest 3** continues that he dislikes it when a girl has too much “guard,” that is, closedness. He emphasizes that it is important to be independent and to have one's own views, but also important to be open to conversation, humble, and willing to resolve things through dialogue. He adds that when choosing a partner it is important that she be ready for sacrifice, both for the relationship and marriage and for the family, which he considers a problem of today's time.

sections.subtitle: The father figure and the identity of the partner
sections.screenshot_description: Host speaks about the relationship with a father; on screen the caption “Father figure”
sections.content:
The host says that in a relationship it matters to him what father figure a girl had in her life and how she relates to her father, if she has one. A father figure does not have to be only a father, but can also be an uncle, aunt, teacher or priest. He emphasizes a healthy measure here, without moving on to other topics.

In his opinion, if a girl does not know what a man should be like, she will project onto her future partner the idea she has of a man. This can lead to the partner trying to be someone he is not, which, in his words, leads to the ruin of the relationship.

**Guest 3** asks whether the host considers this a priority, to which the host answers affirmatively, but notes that not every girl has to have a clearly defined relationship with her father. If she does not, one moves on to other important qualities.

sections.subtitle: Wounds, trust and the question of makeup
sections.screenshot_description: Host speaks about psychological wounds; in the frame a heart icon and the caption “Trust”
sections.content:
The host speaks about psychological wounds and trust. In his words, girls who have been through a traumatic or painful relationship find it hard to open up to a new person. While men often move on quickly after a failure, girls need more time to be ready to open up and share their intimate thoughts with someone.

The host stresses that it is important how a girl communicates her boundaries. She can say that it is hard for her to open up, but that she sees in the partner a person with whom she could one day share her inner intimacy. He calls this approach beautiful and sincere.

He then mentions that female friends can be important to him, but that he could not be in a relationship with a girl who is always available to her friends, that is, one who spends too much time with them. He considers that not normal.

He also expresses personal discomfort with excessive use of makeup. He gives the example of a wedding where he saw several beautiful girls, but was put off by too much makeup. He adds that some “guard” in a girl attracts him, but that he does not like it when it is excessive.

sections.subtitle: The diversity of a person and a healthy balance in a relationship
sections.screenshot_description: Host speaks about diversity; Guest 3 comments on the conclusion about a person who is ready for a relationship
sections.content:
The host concludes that in a partner it matters to him that she be diverse. In his words, it is good for a girl to have hobbies, female friends, activities and a job, and to have her own life. This shows that she is not dependent only on her partner.

The host stresses that he does not want the partner to be his only support, but rather that together with him, with other people, family and faith, she forms a whole. For this reason he compares a healthy relationship with a situation in which the partner is the only source of happiness, which he considers undesirable.

**Guest 3** summarizes that diversity shows how a person works on themselves and how ready they are for a relationship. He adds that one can see whether a person has been waiting for a partner or has truly been preparing for that moment.

sections.subtitle: Realistic expectations or a scale of ideal qualities?
sections.screenshot_description: Host and Female Guest 1 in a debate on standards; on screen the caption “Expectations and standards”
sections.content:
The host asks whether expectations of a partner are realistic or unrealistic, and whether there is some scale of criteria that a partner should meet.

**Female Guest 1** believes that everyone has some criteria and that it would be sad if someone agreed to anything. The problem, however, is that criteria are often too high. She notes that men may have a distorted picture of women because of content on the internet, while women often have similar expectations of men. Instead of looking at the real person in front of them, people list what is missing.

The female guest also warns of the problem of too much choice. Apps and the large number of people in communities create the impression that there is always someone better, so it is hard to make a decision. Therefore, in her words, people should lower their expectations somewhat, but not so much that they fall below the necessary limits.

The host follows up with the difference between an **ideal** and a **standard**. An ideal is what one strives for, while a standard is the boundary below which one does not go.

sections.subtitle: Femininity and masculinity: what are they today?
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 1 and Guest 4 speak about femininity and masculinity; on screen the caption “Femininity and masculinity”
sections.content:
The host suggests that the female guests define what makes a woman feminine, and the guests what makes a man masculine, with the note that there is no universal truth about this.

**Guest 1** (SPEAKER_05) considers it primary that a woman knows how to love. The way that love is expressed in various areas of life shows femininity. He lists openness toward others, readiness to help, the ability to listen, and the right word at the right time. In his words, a woman acquires these virtues through her relationship with God. He adds that every woman has femininity within her, but that it is developed to the extent that a woman cultivates it and works on it.

**Female Guest 1** adds that not every girl is feminine in the same way. Tenderness is expressed differently, so not all women should be reduced to the same model. She stresses that it is important for a woman to know how to let the man lead, but not in the sense of excessive complaining about every small thing.

**Guest 4** believes it is important for a man to be direct and to communicate his intentions clearly, to know where the relationship stands and where it is going. Resoluteness means fulfilling what was promised, and a man should discern how to behave in a relationship, always in prayer and in accordance with the will of God.

sections.subtitle: Faith and marriage as basic expectations
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 3 speaks about faith and marriage; on screen the caption “Faith and marriage”
sections.content:
**Guest 3** returns to the question of expectations and states that among many personal expectations there are ones that Catholics consider fundamental. Among them he singles out openness to faith and to a shared life in God, and openness to life in marriage.

In his opinion, if a person truly loves their partner and cares about them, other things may not be fully aligned, but that should not be a reason to end the relationship. Still, he considers religious and marital foundations indispensable. A relationship without them, in his words, would be very demanding.

Guest 3 concludes that these are expectations one should have a right to, while other things can be adjusted.

sections.subtitle: What a man should be: clear, active, responsible
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 3 and Host discuss the character of a man; on screen the caption “Man”
sections.content:
Guest 3 answers the question of what a man should be like: clear and concrete from the very beginning, capable of setting standards and criteria in a relationship and applying them consistently. He emphasizes that a man should be active, a disciplined person who does not withdraw into passivity, and that he should be an example to his wife and children.

The host adds that a man should be capable of work and of caring for others. As a fundamental trait of masculinity he names the ability to manage on his own in everyday practical tasks, such as changing a light bulb, mowing the grass or assembling furniture. He considers that a man who cannot do these things can hardly be sought as a partner.

The host also criticizes a culture in which people express value through possession: a car, an apartment, a job. In his opinion, such an approach can lead a man to lose his sense of self-worth when he loses these things. He stresses that it is more important to be a person who has integrity than a person who owns something.

sections.subtitle: Consistency in small things as an indicator of character
sections.screenshot_description: Female Guest 1 and Host speak about consistency; the frame shows a humorous illustration of delayed promises
sections.content:
The host speaks about consistency and moral order in a relationship. In his opinion, a man should set boundaries and be consistent in enforcing them. When he is consistent, integrity grows in the relationship.

As an example, he mentions situations in which a partner promises to fix something but never does. The host refers to a suggestion from a female guest who mentioned a car with faults, and a partner who says he will fix the air conditioning but it never happens.

**Female Guest 1** concludes that inconsistency shows up in small things too. If a man says he will do something and does not do it, one can assume that he will not be able to fulfill greater obligations toward his partner and family in the future.

**Guest 3** tells a joke about someone who constantly promises but never delivers, further illustrating the topic.

sections.subtitle: From thinking to a concrete step: how to approach?
sections.screenshot_description: Host asks a question about the first step; on screen the caption “First step”
sections.content:
The host moves on to the practical level: what to do when someone catches your eye, how to approach and how to take the first step so that it passes as painlessly as possible. He asks whether one should go out on the first day and stay until late, or whether one should be satisfied with a short meeting.

**Female Guest 1** believes that people need to understand that the first day is not a marriage or a relationship. The first coffee is simply a get-together that can end with no obligations at all. She warns that people often take the first meeting too seriously, and that unrealistic expectations are therefore created on both sides.

The female guest stresses that one should not think the other person has promised something or that the relationship will immediately develop into marriage. For this reason, everyone should cool down a bit and accept that the first meeting is only a beginning.

sections.subtitle: Coffee, a walk or a longer talk: what a first date looks like
sections.screenshot_description: Host and participants discuss coffee and walks; cups and a board with the caption “First date” are on the table
sections.content:
The host puts forward the view that on a first date one should not go for coffee, because a café is, in his opinion, an unnatural setting for two people who barely know each other. He adds that coffee is usually a single drink that one pays for, and sitting at a table can be awkward if the conversation does not flow.

The host also warns that a first meeting, if it is spent sitting at a table, can last two to three hours, because people have to talk about everyday topics, about school, work and family. In his experience, such a conversation lasts longer than expected.

**Female Guest 1** adds that a walk is more natural for a first day because it puts less pressure on the people talking, and at the same time allows for a more relaxed conversation. She notes that it is easier to talk while walking, but also that during a walk one has to keep talking constantly.

**Guest 3** believes that sitting at a table is more intimate, while a walk can be more pleasant after a first meeting. He stresses that everything depends on whether the people already know each other. For a first meeting, he says, coffee can be a good choice, but it is not the main measure of a relationship.

sections.subtitle: How often to see each other at the beginning?
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 3 speaks about how often people meet; on screen the caption “Frequency of meeting”
sections.content:
The host asks how often one should see each other in the early phase, whether it is necessary to meet five times a week or once or twice a week.

**Guest 3** answers that it depends on the people. If they are already mature people who know what they want and are ready for marriage, it is enough to see each other once or twice a week, taking into account work and life obligations. Younger people, who are in love, may see each other more often.

He gives his own experience as an example: for them it was necessary to spend a lot of time together for things to get going, so they saw each other three to four times a week.

sections.subtitle: Love languages and moderation in attention
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 4 speaks about love languages; on screen the caption “Love languages”
sections.content:
**Guest 4** speaks about how, in the early phase, it is important to talk about how much the other person is interested in us. In his words, the person on the other side may perceive that you like them only if you spend time with them. For some, gifts are important, for others words of praise, and for others quality time.

Guest 4 stresses that it is important to talk about this, but that one should be moderate. One should not give a gift or attention every time, because that can become overwhelming. He concludes that a man should be moderate, perceptive and attentive in a relationship.

sections.subtitle: The belief that one will never meet anyone
sections.screenshot_description: Host asks a question about people who believe they will never find anyone; an illustration of loneliness
sections.content:
The host addresses viewers who are alone and believe they will never find anyone. He calls this one of the greatest lies about dating. He asks whether this is really true and how to encourage people not to give up.

**Guest 4** replies that one needs to create opportunities in one's life and environment. He notes that in women's circles the atmospheres are often more closed, so it is harder to come by opportunities to meet. As an example, he describes a situation at a wedding where a friend waited for someone to invite him to dance, while two women simply got up and started dancing. Such situations show that opportunities can be used if someone decides to take a step.

sections.subtitle: Courage and creativity as a path to getting to know people
sections.screenshot_description: Guest 3 and Guest 2 speak about courage and effort; the caption “Be brave and creative” is shown in the frame
sections.content:
**Female Guest 1** stresses that nothing in life comes by itself. In her words, if you want something, you have to work for it and grit your teeth. She admits that for some people it is natural to be open and to give signals, while for others it is hard. Still, she emphasizes that one has to put in effort.

**Guest 3** advises men to be brave and creative. If it is hard to arrange a one-on-one meeting, they can organize a shared gathering, agree with friends or with a female friend who can help. The important thing, he says, is simply to take a step.

**Guest 2** adds that a girl who feels uninteresting in her circle can step out of her comfort zone, go to new places and meet new people. One should not stay only in the same circle, but should move around and discover new opportunities.

sections.subtitle: Closing messages and encouragement for viewers
sections.screenshot_description: Host says goodbye to viewers in the closing shot of the show; the LaudatoTV logo is on screen
sections.content:
The host closes the show with a brief reminder that a man should gather courage and approach a girl, and that this is a man's job. He calls on the young men not to behave like passive observers.

He then repeats the question for those who are alone and believe they will never meet anyone, and stresses that encouragement is important. He adds that the show has ended and that viewers will see each other in the next episode, after which he says goodbye to the audience.
